planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into fast-draining, lean mineral soil; resents rich garden loam and summer irrigation, both of which cause rot.

directions: A striking scapose annual that sends up stemless, fragrant lavender-to-purple flowers with white throats directly from a basal rosette, this gilia thrives in the harshest, driest garden spots where little else will bloom, and is a strong moth-pollinated nectar source. Because it is scapose, with no true aboveground stem, the rosette sits flat against the soil through winter before the flowering scapes shoot up in spring, so keep nearby plantings low to avoid shading it out. Best used in a dry gravel garden, desert wildflower mix, or Joshua-tree-woodland-themed bed rather than a conventional border.

planting.note: Scatter seed over cleared, lean soil in autumn and let winter rain do the germinating; avoid summer water once bloom finishes.

directions: A compact, free-flowering foothill annual with pink-purple blooms, this gilia fills the gap between early spring bulbs and summer annuals in a dry Mediterranean-climate border, with an erect branching habit that gives a fuller, more upright look than ground-hugging relatives. Its naturally leafy lower stems make a good filler among bunchgrasses or at the base of larger chaparral shrubs. It is a true winter annual and will not persist through hot, irrigated summers, pairing well with other small-flowered Polemoniaceae in a foothill-woodland wildflower mix.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall or very early spring into fast-draining, rocky or sandy soil; amend heavy soil with pumice or coarse grit to mimic its native open montane sites.

directions: Producing an unusually wide color range of pink, yellow, white, and lavender on a single wiry, cobwebby-haired plant, this gilia gives long-season visual variety from one seed packet, well suited to high-elevation rock gardens and dry montane plantings where few annuals perform. It tolerates more elevation and cold than most Gilia species, making it a candidate for high-desert and mountain gardens from Lodgepole to Yellow Pine forest zones. Deadheading is unnecessary since the basal rosette persists while the flowering stems senesce naturally at season's end.

planting.note: Direct-sow in autumn into lean, unimproved soil in full sun, grown in drifts rather than as single specimens since individual flowers are under a centimeter wide.

directions: A fine-textured, airy annual with tiny pale lavender flowers held in open branching clusters, this gilia makes an unobtrusive filler or meadow haze component between bolder wildflowers in a native chaparral-themed planting, strongly attractive to dozens of native bee species. It pairs naturally with other Gilia in a chaparral or coastal-sage-scrub wildflower mix, extending bloom texture without competing for the same visual space. Let the capsules dry and self-sow for return bloom next year.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare, undisturbed soil in fall as a woodland-edge groundcover annual beneath oaks or in dappled understory.

directions: One of the more shade-tolerant Polemoniaceae annuals, genuinely useful under high open woodland canopy where most wildflower-mix species fail, this plant carries pink-to-lavender flowers with contrasting yellow or white throats that read well in mass as underplanting. Its hairy stems sprawl loosely to about a foot, so it works well cascading over a low wall or rock edge. Keep it dry in summer dormancy — it is adapted to a long rainless season.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare soil in autumn; try both part-shade under oaks and open sunny beds given its unusually wide habitat tolerance.

directions: With an extremely wide elevation and habitat tolerance from sea level to nearly 4,000 feet across the Sierra Nevada to the Channel Islands, this is one of the most adaptable small Polemoniaceae annuals for California gardens statewide, with pink or yellow flowers on compact plants suited to rock gardens, path edging, and container sowing. Its tolerance for chaparral, oak woodland, and mixed evergreen and montane coniferous forest means it adapts to more garden situations than most Leptosiphon species. Avoid summer irrigation; its compact size makes it a good choice for small raised beds or rock-garden crevices.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare mineral soil in fall or early spring, massed rather than planted as individual specimens; let it dry out completely after spring bloom.

directions: Tiny bright golden-yellow flowers on a wiry, needle-leaved annual give an unusual warm color note rare among the mostly pink, lavender, and white relatives in this group. Its native range spans Mojave and Sonoran desert flats as well as Peninsular and Transverse Range chaparral and pinyon-juniper woodland, so it tolerates more heat and less winter chill than most of its relatives — a good choice for low- and mid-elevation desert gardens in Arizona, Nevada, and southern California. Give it full sun on bare mineral soil.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto open, undisturbed soil in autumn, giving it its own open patch at the front of a bed since taller companions easily shade it out.

directions: Distinctive fringed-tip pale pink petals with purple basal spots and a yellow-white throat make this one of the most ornamentally refined small annuals in the group, flowering low to the ground in chaparral, coastal-sage-scrub, or valley-grassland-style plantings. This southern-California endemic flowers in winter and early spring, earlier than many of its relatives, so pair it with other winter-blooming natives for continuous color. Allow seed to mature and shatter in place for reliable self-sowing in subsequent years.
